title: Fastest Repair Crew Schedule
statement:
A garage has mechanics with skill ratings ranks. A mechanic with rating r needs r · m² minutes to repair m cars on their own. All mechanics work at the same time, and each car is repaired by exactly one mechanic.

There are cars cars to fix. Split them among the mechanics (some may get none) and return the smallest number of minutes after which every car is repaired.

examples.why: The rating-1 mechanic fixes 3 cars in 9 minutes, the rating-3 mechanic fixes 2 in 12. Giving the fast one 4 cars would take 16.
Time grows with the square, so spreading wins: 2 + 1 + 1 cars takes 8 minutes, while 4 cars on one mechanic takes 32.

hints: Turn the question around: if you are given T minutes, how many cars can the whole crew finish?
In T minutes a mechanic with rating r finishes the largest m with r · m² ≤ T, which is floor(√(T / r)). Adding that over all mechanics is O(n).
More time never means fewer cars, so binary search the smallest T whose total reaches cars. The answer lies between 1 and min(ranks) · cars².

explain.intuition:
Deciding who repairs what is hard to do directly. Checking a guess is easy: with a fixed budget of T minutes, each mechanic simply repairs as many cars as fit, floor(√(T / r)), and you add those up. If the total reaches cars, T is enough.

That check is monotonic: if T minutes are enough, T + 1 are too. So the answers form a "no, no, …, no, yes, yes, …" line, and binary search finds the first "yes". The upper end is safe: the best mechanic alone fixes everything in min(ranks) · cars² minutes.
steps: While lo < hi, take mid and count the cars: the sum over mechanics of floor(√(mid / r)).
If the count reaches cars, mid works, so set hi = mid. Otherwise set lo = mid + 1.
pitfalls: Floating-point square roots near 10<sup>14</sup> can be off by one. Correct the integer root (or use an exact integer square root).
Greedy splitting by rating, such as giving the best mechanic most of the cars. The square makes extra cars on one person expensive, as the second example shows.
Using 32-bit integers: the time can reach 100 · 10<sup>12</sup>.

solutions.title: Hand out cars one at a time with a heap
solutions.idea: Give each next car to the mechanic who would finish it soonest. The last finishing time is the answer. Correct, but it does one heap operation per car.
solutions.py:
class Solution:
    def fastestRepair(self, ranks: List[int], cars: int) -> int:
        # (finish time if this mechanic takes one more car, rank, cars so far)
        h = [(r, r, 0) for r in ranks]
        heapq.heapify(h)
        worst = 0
        for _ in range(cars):
            t, r, m = heapq.heappop(h)
            worst = max(worst, t)
            heapq.heappush(h, (r * (m + 2) ** 2, r, m + 1))
        return worst

solutions.title: Binary search on the time
solutions.idea: For a time budget T, each mechanic fixes floor(√(T / r)) cars. Find the smallest T whose total reaches cars.

solutions.title: Binary search, grouped by rating
solutions.idea: Ratings are at most 100, so count how many mechanics share each rating. The check then costs O(100) instead of O(n).

followups: Each mechanic can work for at most H minutes. How do you report that the cars cannot all be fixed?
Instead of r · m², a mechanic needs r · m minutes. Is binary search still needed, or is there a direct formula?
